title: Fissure sealants & fluoride varnish
blurb: Two professional preventive treatments: sealing pits and fissures, and applying 22,600 ppm fluoride varnish, including how often and the nurse's role.
question: An 8-year-old with a history of decay attends for a check-up. The dentist plans fissure sealants on the newly erupted lower first molars and fluoride varnish on all the teeth. What will you prepare, why is moisture control so important, and how often should the varnish be repeated?

teach.h: Two treatments, two ways of protecting
teach.body: Fissure sealants and fluoride varnish are both professional preventive treatments, but they protect teeth in different ways. A sealant is a physical barrier: it fills the deep grooves on the biting surfaces of back teeth so plaque can't settle there. Varnish is a chemical boost: it coats every surface with a high concentration of fluoride, which helps enamel resist acid and remineralise. Many children need both.

teach.caption: Decay starting in a deep fissure on a molar's biting surface and spreading into the dentine. Bristles can't reach the bottom of narrow fissures, so plaque sits there undisturbed.

teach.body: Sealants are placed on the pits and fissures of permanent molars (and sometimes premolars) as soon as possible after they erupt, when they are most vulnerable: first permanent molars around age 6, second molars around age 12. DBOH strongly recommends resin sealant on permanent teeth on eruption for children and young people giving concern. Resin-based sealants are the most retentive. Glass ionomer may be used when a tooth is only partly erupted and keeping it dry is difficult.

steps.label: Isolate
steps.sub: Cotton rolls, dry guards or rubber dam

steps.label: Etch
steps.sub: Phosphoric acid gel on the fissures

steps.label: Check
steps.sub: Probe for retention; check the bite

teach.caption: Placed by the dentist, therapist or hygienist. You prepare the materials, keep the field dry with suction and cotton rolls, and protect eyes from the curing light.

teach.body: Fluoride varnish is 2.26% sodium fluoride, which is 22,600 ppm fluoride. It is painted onto the teeth, sets on contact with saliva and releases fluoride over the following hours. DBOH strongly recommends it twice a year for all children from age 3, two or more times a year for children giving concern, and twice a year for adults giving concern. A dental nurse who has had the extra training can apply it, but only on a dentist's prescription (or patient specific direction).

items: Check there is a written prescription and that you are trained to apply it.
Check the medical history: varnish such as Duraphat contains colophony, so don't use it if the patient is allergic (ask about reactions to sticking plasters).
Explain the treatment and gain valid consent (from a parent for young children).
Remove excess plaque and saliva and dry the teeth with cotton rolls or gauze.
Paint a thin layer onto all surfaces, starting with the most at-risk areas.
Give the product's aftercare advice, and record the product, batch number and prescriber in the notes.

teach.h: Sealant vs varnish at a glance

rows.label: Who applies
values: Clinician, or trained nurse on prescription

teach.text: Moisture is the enemy of a resin sealant. If saliva touches the etched enamel, the sealant won't bond and may fall off. The surface must be washed, dried and etched again before applying it.

items: Sealants physically block pits and fissures; place them as soon as possible after the permanent molars erupt.
Sequence: clean, isolate, etch, wash and dry, apply and cure, check retention and bite.
Varnish is 2.26% NaF = 22,600 ppm; twice a year for all children 3+, 2 or more times if giving concern.
Check for colophony allergy before applying varnish.
Nurses can apply varnish with training, only on prescription.

summary: You can now explain how fissure sealants and fluoride varnish protect teeth, say which teeth are sealed and when, list the steps for placing a sealant and why moisture control matters, give DBOH varnish frequencies, apply varnish safely within your scope, and spot the colophony allergy contraindication.

A.q: Which teeth are most commonly fissure sealed?
A.why: Newly erupted permanent molars have deep pits and fissures that trap plaque, so they benefit most from sealing.

whyNot.0: Incisors have smooth surfaces without deep fissures.
whyNot.1: Canines have no occlusal fissures to seal.
whyNot.3: Deciduous incisors don't have fissures; sealants target molar fissures.

A.q: What concentration of fluoride does fluoride varnish contain?
A.why: Fluoride varnish is 2.26% sodium fluoride, which is 22,600 ppm fluoride.

whyNot.0: 1,450 ppm is a standard family toothpaste.
whyNot.1: 5,000 ppm is a prescription toothpaste for those aged 16 and over.
whyNot.2: 2,800 ppm is a prescription toothpaste for those aged 10 and over.

A.q: During sealant placement, saliva contaminates the etched enamel. What should happen next?
options: Wash, dry and re-etch the tooth
Blow air on it and continue
A.why: Saliva contamination prevents the resin bonding, so the tooth must be washed, dried and etched again.

whyNot.1: The sealant wouldn't bond to contaminated enamel and would likely fail.
whyNot.2: Drying alone doesn't remove the saliva coating from the etched surface.
whyNot.3: More sealant doesn't fix a poor bond.

B.q: How often does DBOH recommend fluoride varnish for a healthy 4-year-old?
B.why: DBOH strongly recommends fluoride varnish twice a year for all children aged 3 to 6.

whyNot.0: Once a year is below the recommended frequency.
whyNot.3: Varnish is advised for all children from 3, not just those with decay.

B.q: Before applying fluoride varnish, which allergy should you check the medical history for?
B.why: Some varnishes such as Duraphat contain colophony, a resin that can cause allergic reactions.

whyNot.0: Latex allergy matters for gloves and dam, but isn't the varnish ingredient of concern.
whyNot.1: Penicillin is an antibiotic, not a component of fluoride varnish.
whyNot.3: Shellfish allergy isn't linked to fluoride varnish.

B.q: What does the etched enamel look like once it has been washed and dried, ready for a sealant?
B.why: Correctly etched and dried enamel has a frosty, chalky white appearance.

whyNot.0: A shiny surface suggests the enamel hasn't been etched.
whyNot.1: Brown staining suggests decay or stain, not etched enamel.
whyNot.2: Pink translucency isn't a sign of etched enamel.

C.q: A trained dental nurse is asked to apply fluoride varnish. What must be in place first?
C.why: Dental nurses with additional training can apply fluoride varnish only on a dentist's prescription.

whyNot.1: Reception staff can't authorise a clinical treatment.
whyNot.2: A patient's request doesn't replace a prescription.
whyNot.3: Plaque doesn't need to be zero; excess plaque is simply removed before applying.

C.q: How do fissure sealants prevent caries?
options: They release high levels of fluoride
They kill bacteria in the saliva
They block plaque from the fissures
C.why: Sealants fill pits and fissures, forming a physical barrier so plaque can't collect there.

whyNot.0: Releasing fluoride is how varnish works; resin sealants mainly act as a barrier.
whyNot.1: Sealants don't kill bacteria in saliva.
whyNot.3: Sealants sit on the enamel surface and don't harden dentine.

C.q: When is the best time to seal the first permanent molars?
C.why: Molars are most vulnerable soon after eruption, so sealing early, around age 6 for first molars, gives the most protection.

whyNot.0: First permanent molars haven't erupted by age 2; it is the baby molars that arrive then.
whyNot.2: By 18 the most vulnerable years have passed.
whyNot.3: Sealants are preventive and placed before decay develops.

reteach.title: A raincoat and a vitamin
reteach.question: If a sealant is like putting a waterproof cover over a gap in a roof, what is fluoride varnish like?

blocks.h: Cover the gap, strengthen the whole roof
blocks.body: A fissure sealant is like a waterproof patch over the deepest cracks in a roof: it physically stops anything getting in, but only where it's placed. Fluoride varnish is more like a weatherproof treatment for the whole roof: it doesn't block the cracks, but it makes every tile tougher and helps small damage repair itself. The patch is placed once and checked; the treatment needs repeating, at least twice a year.

blocks.caption: The occlusal (biting) surface, with its pits and fissures, is the surface sealed.

blocks.text: Sealant = barrier on fissures only. Varnish = fluoride on every surface. Don't swap their mechanisms in an exam answer.

explain.body: Seal the pits and fissures of permanent molars as soon as possible after eruption: first molars around 6, second molars around 12. Resin is most retentive; glass ionomer helps when moisture control is difficult.

test.q: A first permanent molar is only partly erupted and hard to keep dry. Which sealant material might the dentist choose?
test.why: Glass ionomer tolerates moisture better than resin, so it can be used as a temporary sealant on partly erupted teeth.

whyNot.1: Zinc oxide eugenol is a temporary filling material, not a sealant.
whyNot.2: Amalgam is a filling material and isn't used to seal fissures.
whyNot.3: Calcium hydroxide is a lining material, not a sealant.

explain.body: Clean, isolate, etch, wash and dry until frosty, apply and light-cure, then check retention with a probe and the bite with articulating paper. Moisture control decides whether it lasts.

test.q: Which step comes straight after etching the fissures?
test.why: After etching, the acid is washed off and the tooth dried until the enamel looks frosty white.

whyNot.0: Curing comes after the sealant has been applied.
whyNot.1: The bite is checked at the very end.
whyNot.3: The etchant must be washed off and the tooth dried before sealant goes on.

explain.body: Varnish is 22,600 ppm fluoride (2.26% NaF). Twice a year for all children from 3; two or more times a year for children giving concern; twice a year for adults giving concern.

items.label: a year for all children aged 3+
times a year if giving concern

test.q: A 10-year-old has active decay and is giving concern. How often does DBOH advise fluoride varnish?
options: Once every two years at recall
Two or more times a year
test.why: For children and young people giving concern, DBOH advises fluoride varnish two or more times a year.

whyNot.0: Every two years is far too infrequent.
whyNot.1: Once a year is below even the advice for all children.
whyNot.2: Varnish isn't tied to a single age.

explain.body: Prescription in place, medical history checked (colophony allergy), consent gained, teeth dried, thin layer applied, aftercare given, product and batch recorded.

test.q: A parent mentions their child reacts badly to sticking plasters. Why does this matter before applying varnish?
options: It suggests a true fluoride allergy
It shows the child is anxious
test.why: Some plasters contain colophony, which is also in some fluoride varnishes, so a reaction suggests the varnish should be avoided.

whyNot.0: True fluoride allergy is not what plaster reactions point to.
whyNot.3: This is about an allergy, not anxiety.
